Elisha (the Prophet)
ee-LYE-shuh
proper noun
Hebrew Elīshā’, “my God is salvation”; from El (God) and yāsha’ (to save).

Biblical Definition

Elisha the son of Shaphat was the prophet who succeeded Elijah, called from the plough as he was breaking the twelfth yoke of oxen, and clothed with a double portion of his master’s spirit when Elijah was taken up in the whirlwind. He took up the fallen mantle, divided Jordan, and ministered in Israel through the reigns of several kings of the northern kingdom. His was a ministry crowded with mercy and with signs: he healed the bitter waters of Jericho with salt, multiplied the widow’s oil, raised the Shunammite’s son, healed Naaman the Syrian leper in the Jordan, made the iron axe-head swim, and fed a hundred men with twenty loaves. Many of these wonders prefigure the greater ministry of Christ, who cleansed lepers, raised the dead, and fed the multitudes. Elisha also saw the unseen armies of the LORD, the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire, and prayed that his servant’s eyes might be opened. He died of sickness, yet his very bones gave life to a dead man cast into his grave, a final witness that the God of resurrection was with him. The dictionary honors him as a true prophet of mercy in an apostate kingdom.

Webster 1828 Definition

The prophet who succeeded Elijah, received a double portion of his spirit, and wrought many miracles of mercy in the northern kingdom, several of them foreshadowing the works of Christ.

expand to see more

ELISHA, n. [Hebrew, my God is salvation.] The disciple and successor of Elijah in the prophetic office.

Called from following the plough, he left all and followed the prophet, ministering to him until his master’s ascension.

Endued with a double portion of Elijah’s spirit, he wrought more recorded miracles than any prophet before Christ.

His wonders—cleansing the leper, raising the dead, multiplying bread—stand as types of the works of the Lord Jesus.

A prophet to the apostate northern kingdom, he held forth the mercy of God amid the idolatry of the house of Ahab and Jehu.

Key Scripture

2Ki 2:9 — "And it came to pass, when they were gone over, that Elijah said unto Elisha, Ask what I shall do for thee, before I be taken away from thee. And Elisha said, I pray thee, let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me."

2Ki 2:14 — "And he took the mantle of Elijah that fell from him, and smote the waters, and said, Where is the LORD God of Elijah? and when he also had smitten the waters, they parted hither and thither: and Elisha went over."

2Ki 6:17 — "And Elisha prayed, and said, LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see. And the LORD opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha."

2Ki 5:14 — "Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean."

Modern Corruption

Rationalist readers strip Elisha’s miracles of their reality, reducing them to legend or folk-tale.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the God of Elisha is the living God who does wonders, and that His mercies in the prophet’s hand point forward to Christ. The cleansing of Naaman by sevenfold washing in Jordan is held up by the Lord Jesus Himself as a rebuke to unbelieving Israel and a sign of grace reaching the Gentile; to empty it of history is to lose its gospel.

Where modern handling errs, it is in the rationalist refusal of the miraculous—the assumption that the axe-head could not swim, the dead could not rise, and the chariots of fire were a poetic flourish. The dictionary receives the narrative as sober history. The same power that opened the servant’s eyes to the mountain full of horses and chariots is the power that raised Jesus from the dead, and the believer is taught by Elisha to reckon the unseen armies of God more real than the visible host of the enemy.

Hebrew Roots

The name confesses that salvation belongs to God, a fitting banner over a ministry of delivering mercy.

expand to see more

Hebrew El — God, the Mighty One; the first element of the name.

Hebrew yāsha’ — to save, deliver; the same root that stands in Isaiah, Joshua, and Jesus.

Together: “my God is salvation,” a name nearly synonymous in sense with the name of the Saviour.

The doubled prophetic office—Elijah then Elisha—mirrors the law and the gospel, judgment and mercy.

Greek Elisaios preserves the name in the Septuagint and in our Lord’s reference in Luke four.

Usage

"Elisha’s miracles are preached as types of Christ’s healings and raisings."

"The opening of the servant’s eyes is a standard text for the reality of the unseen warfare and the protection of God."

"Naaman’s washing in Jordan is used to teach the simplicity and offense of the gospel’s appointed way."
